lessons.title: Convolution, shapes and weight sharing
lessons.intro: A convolutional layer is a dense layer with two constraints: each output sees only a small window, and every window uses the same weights. This lesson covers what the layer really computes (cross-correlation), the output-size formula you must be able to apply without a framework, and why weight sharing gives translation equivariance.
takeaways: Output side = floor((n + 2p - k) / s) + 1; dilation widens the kernel to d(k - 1) + 1.
Weight sharing: translation equivariance and far fewer parameters, with the same expressiveness limits of a constrained dense layer.
Backward: dK sums over positions, dX is a full convolution; overlapping windows accumulate.
lessons.trap: Calling convolution 'translation invariant'. It is equivariant; invariance needs pooling or a global reduction, and even then only approximately.

sections.heading: Cross-correlation, not convolution
sections.text: Deep-learning 'convolutions' slide the kernel over the input without flipping it. The difference is invisible for learned kernels but shows up when you port hand-made filters or compare with np.convolve.

sections.heading: The output-size formula
sections.text: Along each axis the output has floor((n + 2p - k) / s) + 1 positions, with dilation d replacing k by d(k - 1) + 1. Work through a few cases by hand before trusting a framework error message.

sections.heading: Weight sharing means equivariance
sections.text: The same filter is applied at every position, so shifting the input shifts the feature map by the same amount. Pooling or a global reduction on top is what turns this into (approximate) invariance.

sections.heading: Gradients of a convolution
sections.text: The kernel gradient sums dy[i] x x[i + j] over all positions; the input gradient is a full convolution of dy with the kernel. Implementations build both from the same sliding windows (im2col) and fold the result back with +=, because overlapping windows contribute to the same pixel.
code: dk = np.array([(dy * x[j:j + 3]).sum() for j in range(2)])

lessons.title: Receptive fields, pooling and the cost of a conv net
lessons.intro: Interviewers ask you to size a conv net on a whiteboard: how big an area does a unit see, what does pooling do in the backward pass, and where do the parameters and the FLOPs go. All of it is arithmetic you can do exactly.
takeaways: Receptive field grows by (k - 1) x jump per layer; strides multiply the jump.
Max pool: gradient to the arg-max only. Average pool: even split.
Params do not depend on image size, MACs scale with H x W; 1 MAC = 2 FLOPs.
Depthwise-separable and 1x1 bottlenecks cut FLOPs; measure real latency as well.
lessons.trap: Quoting FLOPs as if they were latency, or counting the parameters of a flattened dense head as if the conv layers were the expensive part.

sections.heading: Receptive field and jump
sections.text: Each layer adds (k - 1) x jump pixels to the receptive field, and a stride multiplies the jump for every later layer. Three plain 3x3 layers see 7x7; a stride-2 layer in the middle makes the last layer count double.
code: print('k', k, 'stride', s, '-> rf', rf, 'jump', jump)
sections.output:
k 3 stride 1 -> rf 3 jump 1
k 3 stride 2 -> rf 5 jump 2
k 3 stride 1 -> rf 9 jump 2

sections.heading: Max pooling routes the gradient
sections.text: Backward through a max pool sends the whole gradient to the arg-max of each window; average pooling spreads it evenly. Overlapping windows accumulate into the same pixel.

sections.heading: Parameters versus compute
sections.text: Parameters are independent of the image size; MACs are not: each output value costs (cin / groups) x kh x kw. High-resolution early layers dominate compute, wide late layers and dense heads dominate parameters.
code: print(h, 'params', cout * cin * k * k + cout, 'MACs', cout * h * h * cin * k * k)

sections.heading: Cheaper layers
sections.text: A depthwise 3x3 plus a 1x1 pointwise convolution costs about 1/k^2 + 1/c of a standard convolution; a 1x1 bottleneck shrinks channels before an expensive 3x3. Cheaper in FLOPs does not always mean faster on hardware, where memory traffic often dominates.
code: sep = c * k * k + c * c

lessons.title: Building and training a CNN
lessons.intro: The architecture decisions that come up in interviews: where to normalise, why skip connections work, how to end the network without tying it to one resolution, how to augment safely and how to fine-tune a pretrained backbone.
takeaways: BatchNorm2d: statistics per channel over N, H, W; eval mode uses running stats.
Residual: gradient 1 + f' on the skip; plain deep stacks are harder to optimise.
Global average pooling decouples the head from input resolution.
Fine-tune: new head first, then the backbone at a much smaller learning rate; augmentations must preserve labels.
lessons.trap: Adding a flip or rotation augmentation without asking whether it can change the class, then reading the accuracy drop as 'the model is bad'.

sections.heading: Normalise per channel
sections.text: BatchNorm2d keeps one mean and variance per channel across batch and spatial axes. GroupNorm and LayerNorm avoid the batch dependence when batches are small.

sections.heading: Skip connections and global pooling
sections.text: A residual block adds its input back, so the derivative along the skip is 1 + f'. Ending with global average pooling makes the head independent of the input size and removes the huge flatten layer.

sections.heading: Augment without changing the label
sections.text: Crops, small shifts, colour jitter and noise preserve most labels; flips and rotations do not for handed shapes, text or digits like 6 and 9. Augment the training set only.
